title: Toll fraud, E911, recording, and QoS
summary: Defensive operations: source restrictions, emergency location, disclosed SIPREC, and the EF PHB.

lessons.title: The toll-fraud class, stated defensively
lessons.summary: Four exposure classes, source restrictions, and caller-identity as a separate control.
objectives: Name the four exposure classes
Point prevention at source restrictions and the numbering plan
Keep STIR identity separate from the trusted list

illustration.title: Class and the control that answers it
illustration.caption: Recognition and prevention. This lesson does not build the sessions it warns about.
rows: Signaling from an address you did not list
A pattern broader than the numbering plan
Patterns that match only intended destinations
Completions the plan did not include
Routes and alarms aligned to the plan

paragraphs: Toll fraud here means billable sessions the enterprise did not intend. The four situations you classify are unauthenticated INVITEs from the public internet, digest passwords that are short or shared or still at a vendor default, dial-peers whose destination pattern matches more numbers than the numbering plan, and routes that can complete calls to international destinations outside that plan.

The job in this lesson is to recognize the class and close it. You list the addresses allowed to present signaling, you make each dial-peer match the plan, and you alarm when completions fall outside the plan. The ladder below is a normal call among the lab addresses. It is the path you intend to keep.

Source restrictions mean inbound VoIP signaling is accepted from addresses you listed. In this lab those documentation addresses are 203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.20, 198.51.100.30, and 192.0.2.40. On the border, the usual remote sources are the call agent at 198.51.100.30 and the carrier at 192.0.2.40.

401 and 407 remain the SIP challenges from RFC 3261, with the digest algorithm work in RFC 7616. The secret is operational: unique, long, and stored as a secret. This lesson does not print a password, a hash, or a default.

sections.h: Authenticated caller ID is a second control
paragraphs: The FCC call-authentication page is the public context for authenticated caller ID. RFC 8224 is the SIP authenticated-identity specification in this library. Together they describe signing calling identity for the providers who verify it.

Identity and the trusted list answer different questions. STIR speaks to who the calling identity claims to be. The trusted list speaks to which addresses may present VoIP signaling into the PBX. Keep both, and let the CME and SRST pages own the list procedure for those products.

lessons.title: Trusted addresses and source restrictions
lessons.summary: The IP address trusted list is per product page. CME and SRST do not share one list size.
objectives: Apply the trusted-list commands as a teaching snippet
Refuse a single universal list size
Keep source restrictions on the lab addresses

illustration.title: What the snippet is
illustration.caption: A border trusts the call agent and the carrier. Phones register to the call agent.

layers.name: List size
layers.detail: Read the page for the product. Quote no shared maximum.

paragraphs: Under voice service voip, ip address trusted authenticate turns on the check, and ip address trusted list holds the addresses allowed to present inbound VoIP calls. The teaching snippet lists 198.51.100.30 and 192.0.2.40. That is the call agent and the carrier in this lab, which is the usual pair on a border element.

The CME toll-fraud page is the procedure for CME, including how an address that fails the check is disconnected on the release that page describes. Copy the cause and the show commands from that page for the release you run. This lesson does not paste a customer log of a disconnect.

SRST trusted IP authentication has its own document. The list size on that page and the list size on the CME page are not one number, so this lesson quotes neither as universal. When you build a lab for SRST, follow the SRST page.

Source restrictions sit beside the list. The interfaces that accept SIP should be the ones facing addresses you operate or an agreed carrier. Adding a host is a change window of its own: one address, then a test call from that address, then stop.

lessons.title: Emergency calling, location, and the FCC page
lessons.summary: Service URN, location conveyance, and the FCC MLTS page. State PSAP rules are not invented here.
objectives: Use urn:service:sos from RFC 5031
Carry location as RFC 6442 and RFC 6881 require
Point national MLTS duties at the FCC page

illustration.title: What the INVITE has to carry
illustration.caption: The synthetic ladder shows the URN and the header name. It does not invent a civic address or a state route.

layers.name: urn:service:sos
layers.detail: RFC 5031 service URN. RFC 6881 is the BCP.

layers.name: FCC MLTS
layers.detail: Kari's Law and RAY BAUM's Act, on the FCC page

sections.h: The service URN and the BCP
paragraphs: Emergency calling uses the service URN urn:service:sos, defined in RFC 5031. RFC 6881 is the Best Current Practice for communications services in support of emergency calling. The Request-URI on the synthetic INVITE is that URN.

Enterprise SIP has to carry location according to those documents and the current national rules. This lesson does not invent a state PSAP procedure, a PSAP address, or a civic record. The production location value is the one those documents and the national rules describe.

RFC 6442 specifies location conveyance for SIP, including the Geolocation header. The ladder shows Geolocation and Geolocation-Routing so you can see the header names. The cid body is not attached. A real request carries the location by value or by reference the way RFC 6442 specifies.

Read the location as part of the emergency request, on the same Call-ID as the INVITE. A call that reaches an emergency route without location has missed this requirement even if a 100 Trying came back.

The FCC MLTS page covers Kari's Law and RAY BAUM's Act. Kari's Law is the federal direct-dial and notification duty. RAY BAUM's Act is the federal dispatchable-location duty. Use the FCC page for the wording and for any update.

National rules change on that page, not in this lesson. When you design enterprise SIP, the request carries the service URN and the location, and the operator confirms the current FCC MLTS requirements before the design is called done.

lessons.title: Disclosed recording with SIPREC
lessons.summary: RFC 7866 is the recording protocol. RFC 7865 is the metadata. Notice and retention are legal questions.
objectives: Name SRC and SRS roles at a high level
Keep metadata with RFC 7865
Treat notice and retention as outside the RFC

illustration.title: A disclosed fork
illustration.caption: The SBC may fork a session to a recording server. The parties are told.

layers.name: SRS
layers.detail: Recording server. The SBC can act as the client that forks.

paragraphs: RFC 7866 is the session recording protocol. An SBC may fork a session to a recording server, the SRS, acting as the recording client. That fork is a SIP session of its own, with its own Call-ID, beside the call the parties are on.

RFC 7865 is the metadata for that recording session. This lesson does not paste a metadata document. When you need a field, read 7865. The synthetic INVITE below shows the fork toward srs.example.com and stops there.

sections.h: Disclosed use, and the legal line
paragraphs: The recording in this lesson is disclosed quality monitoring and compliance. The participants are on notice under the program that authorized the recording. The ladder is that architecture.

Notice and retention rules are legal questions. They sit outside RFC 7866 and RFC 7865. The RFC tells you how the SBC and the SRS exchange the session and the metadata. Counsel and the retention schedule tell you whether you may record and how long you may keep it.

lessons.title: Voice, EF, and what the PHB does not design
lessons.summary: RFC 3246 defines the EF PHB. RFC 4594 maps telephony to EF. This lesson does not design a LAN.
objectives: Name EF as the PHB for the telephony class
Keep the recommended codepoint inside the RFC
Leave switch queues and campus design out of the lesson

illustration.title: What this lesson claims
illustration.caption: Voice media follows the telephony mapping. Signaling is a different service class in RFC 4594, and this table does not assign it a codepoint.
rows: The one RFC 3246 prints for EF

paragraphs: RFC 3246 defines the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior. It recommends a codepoint for that PHB. Use the value printed in the RFC when you mark voice media, and say that you took it from RFC 3246.

RFC 4594 is the configuration guideline for DiffServ service classes. In that guidance the telephony service class is mapped to EF. Voice media is the traffic this lesson marks that way. The SIP messages you debug are not the same service class, and this lesson does not assign them a codepoint from memory.

The call ladder ends in RTP on the addresses and ports in SDP. Those RTP packets are what the telephony mapping applies to. A 200 OK does not itself mark packets. The marking is a network behavior on the media path after the answer.

This lesson does not invent a LAN design, a queue depth, a switch policy, or a campus diagram. The operator's approved design is where those decisions live. If the voice is marked EF and still suffers, the next evidence is loss and delay on that path, not a new SIP status code.

lessons.title: Alarms that match the failure
lessons.summary: Alarm on OPTIONS, TLS expiry, 503, recording-session failure, and trusted-list rejects. Each alarm names its document.
objectives: Tie each alarm to one failure class
Use OPTIONS as a liveness signal
Keep synthetic examples labeled synthetic

illustration.title: Alarm path
illustration.caption: Page someone with the class, the Call-ID if there is one, and the document.

paragraphs: OPTIONS to a trunk that stops answering is a liveness alarm. RFC 3261 section 11 defines OPTIONS. A burst of 503 Service Unavailable is a server-side alarm, often with Retry-After. Certificate expiry and a TLS version below the peer's floor are handshake alarms, and toward Teams that floor is TLS 1.2.

A SIPREC session to the SRS that fails is a recording alarm. Cite RFC 7866 for the session and keep notice and retention on the legal schedule. A trusted-list reject is an operations alarm: confirm the listed addresses against the CME or SRST page for the product, using the lab pair 198.51.100.30 and 192.0.2.40 when this border is the teaching snippet.

A useful page names the class, the synthetic or real identifier you are allowed to share, and the next single check. For a SIP failure include Call-ID and the status code. For a handshake failure say that no SIP status came back, and name mismatch, CA, or version.
Examples in this lesson are synthetic. A customer syslog stays in the customer's system. The alarm text you practice with uses example.com and the documentation addresses only.

lessons.title: One change in the window
lessons.summary: Freeze the baseline, change one variable, verify, and keep the previous snippet ready.
objectives: Record a baseline before the change
Change a single variable
Verify with one signal and roll back that variable

illustration.title: The window
illustration.caption: Rollback is the previous value of the one variable you touched.

paragraphs: A change window starts from a baseline you can name: the last OPTIONS 200, the current trusted-list snippet, or the current codec offer. Write that down in the ticket with the lab addresses you are using.

Then change one variable. One new ipv4 line, or one codec in the offer, or one TLS setting. A window that edits the trusted list, the dial-peers, and the certificate template together cannot tell you which edit fixed or broke the call.

sections.h: Verify, then stop or roll back
paragraphs: Verification is one signal. A test call to +15551212 among the lab addresses, or a fresh OPTIONS to 192.0.2.40, or a 200 that replaces a 503. Success is that signal, not a feeling that the config looks complete.

Rollback puts back the previous value of the same variable. Keep the teaching snippet's previous form in the ticket. Customer logs stay out of the practice record. Synthetic Call-IDs are enough to show the method.
